florid

/FLOR-id/ - the stress falls on FLOR · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Florid means flowery, ornate.

His thank-you note ran two florid pages when one plain sentence would have done.

Example

The listing described a modest bungalow in florid prose — 'a jewel-box sanctuary bathed in dawn's first amber' — and the buyers who pulled up to the plain little porch felt swindled by adjectives.

Florid is more exact than 'wordy' because the problem isn't length, it's decoration: the sentence is dressed in curls and blossoms of language. A long plain paragraph is merely wordy; ten words wearing perfume and lace are florid.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

flowery: Flowery is the everyday word for dressed-up language, and it is the gentler charge — a few blossoms too many. Florid is stronger and more formal: the whole style is in full ornamental flower, decoration crowding out substance line after line.

high-flown: High-flown language reaches upward — grand, lofty phrases straining to sound important. Florid decorates instead: curls, blossoms, and perfumed flourishes laid over the sentence. A high-flown speech aims too high; a florid one is dressed too richly, and a passage can easily be both.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

plain: saying it simply, without ornament

understated: deliberately quieter than it could be

Where it sits · how heavily decorated the style is

fancy → florid → overwrought

fancy vs. florid: Fancy is a few dressy touches — it stops well short of florid.

overwrought vs. florid: Overwrought goes further than florid: the ornament turns to strain, every line overloaded past bearing.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — flor-: flower (Latin flos, floris)

Suffix — -id: adjective ending: full of, having the quality of

Put it together: Flor- (flower) + -id (full of) = covered in flowers. Latin flos, floris planted a garden across English — flora, floral, flourish — and florid is what style becomes when blossoms sprout on every phrase: literally 'flowered' language.

Use the root in a new word: florist: Critics date the movement's efflorescence to a single Paris season.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / critical

Florid is mostly for style — speech, prose, lettering, music — and it usually carries a raised eyebrow: decoration has gotten ahead of substance. Its neighbor ornate does the same work for physical objects (an ornate frame, a florid speech), and garish adds the charge of clashing bad taste. Florid can also describe a flushed red complexion; that older sense is worth recognizing on sight.
